I’ve farmed these 4.5 mu in Quzhou for 30 years, and at 48 I know every piece of this land. With just my wife and me, I can’t run around managing six crops on six different schedules, so I organize my year around what is reliable. My cabbage–eggplant rotation on 2 mu is my backbone: I will rotary-till and plant hybrid spring cabbage as soon as the soil warms, because cabbage pays early if the heads are tight and clean. I irrigate from my well—spring rain is never enough here—and I watch for diamondback moth; three careful sprays are enough if you scout daily. Come June, once the cabbage is out, I immediately till again and set out hybrid eggplant seedlings. Eggplant feeds heavy, so I push nitrogen and potassium, and I will water seven times through the hot months because my well gives me that security. 

For the rest of the land, I keep it simple. Half a mu of kidney bean in spring—traditional seed, low fertilizer, easy pick. Half a mu of chili; I use an improved local variety because hybrid seed is too costly for such a small patch, and I keep water steady so the fruit sets thick. One full mu I leave for autumn cauliflower; I never plant cauliflower in spring here because the heat makes it bolt and the market floods with poor heads. Autumn cauliflower is firm and sweet, and I can nurse it through September with four good irrigations. Finally, half a mu of overwintering spinach goes in late autumn; it sleeps through winter and gives me the first fresh greens of next year, which always fetch a good price at the village market. I do not plough deep—rotary tillage is fast and keeps my soil structure right for vegetables. That is my year.
